newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Asian Sugar - China harvest begins, rest of Asia flat.
newsitem.headline: Asian Sugar - China harvest begins, rest of Asia flat.

text.p: The full effect of summer typhoons and the ability of the Beijing government to control imports are the major factors now facing the Chinese sugar industry, traders and industry executives said on Wednesday.
Prices in China's major sugar-producing region of Guangxi had begun to recover, a Western executive with milling interests in the southwestern region said.
Ex-factory prices were now around 4,300 yuan (US$518) a tonne, he said, above break-even point for most local producers.
Cane prices had been set between 230 and 300 yuan ($27 and $36) per tonne. Ten tonnes of cane produces one tonne of sugar.
If prices fell below 4,000 yuan ($482), the industry would face another year of losses, traders and industry sources said.

This was the case in 1995 when more than three million tonnes of sugar was imported, most of it illegally, to fill a perceived shortfall between the 5.65 million tonne harvest and demand of more than eight million tonnes.
A government effort to keep a tight grip on sugar imports would have a direct impact on the success of the industry this season, sources said.
"There is the political will there and the signs are good but you can't eat promises. We are still at the behest of how effective these promises are in execution," the Western executive said.

Industry sources said China was not expected to begin importing sugar until the second half of 1997 -- timing that coincides with the Australian season -- and then could need 1.5 million to two million tonnes.
Australia sold 355,000 tonnes of sugar to China last year, almost half the 1994 tonnage because of the import crackdown.
An Australian industry source said Cuba remained the wild card in the Chinese supply picture.
"I don't think Cuban sugar would come at favourable prices for the Chinese, but they may be treated favourably in terms of market access," he said on condition of anonymity.
China's total sugar output has been put at 6.6 million tonnes for the 1996-97 crop currently under harvest.
However, a force 15 typhoon that swept through Guangxi in late summer could have damaged up to five percent of the cane crop there, the Western source said.

The gales had not uprooted cane plants, he said, but had flattened them and this could lead to a decrease in sugar content, either through direct damage or the need to cut the plants in two during the harvest.
This in turn could help buoy prices, trade sources said.
Crushing in Guangxi, expected to produce 2.6 million tonnes, should begin next week, with the harvest continuing until March.
Elsewhere in Asia, Japanese sugar traders said they expected the raw sugar market to remain quiet in the near term due to a lack of buying activity.

Premiums for Thai raw sugar for March/May delivery were quoted at around 0.50/0.60 cents (bid/offer) per pound over the most active March futures on New York's Coffee, Sugar and Cocoa Exchange (CSCE) FOB basis.
This is down from about 0.65/0.80 cents a week earlier.
January/March delivery was quoted at 0.75/0.90 cents over New York futures, while May/July were 0.50/0.60 cents over New York.
"Thai premiums are easing further on a lack of buying, and this trend will remain until the end of this year," a sugar trader at a major trade house said.
Traders said they were watching to see if the delay in crushing at some mills in Thailand -- due to begin on November 5 but held up by this weekend's general election -- would affect shipments.
"Chances are sugar shipments during December and January could be affected by the delayed crushing, but we're not sure at this stage," another sugar trader in Tokyo said.
-- Lynne O'Donnell, Hong Kong Newsroom (852) 2843 6470
-- Eiichiro Tokumoto, Tokyo Newsroom (81-3) 3432 7391
